Test whether prevalence differs between two groups

Source: R/test_difference.R
test_difference.Rd

Analysis function: given the number of positives and the number tested in two groups, tests whether their true prevalence differs. Returns the estimated difference with the confidence interval that matches the test, the p-value and whether the difference is significant. It is the analysis twin of design_difference().

The test compares the measured (apparent) prevalences, the share who test positive. Because sensitivity and specificity are assumed the same in both groups, the measured prevalences differ exactly when the true ones do, in the same direction, so the p-value does not depend on sensitivity or specificity. Only the reported difference and its interval are corrected for an imperfect test (Rogan-Gladen correction). Clustering is handled with a design effect for each group.

Hypotheses (\(p_1\), \(p_2\) are the true prevalences):

"two.sided" (default)

H0: \(p_1 = p_2\) against H1: \(p_1 \ne p_2\).

"greater"

H0: \(p_1 \le p_2\) against H1: \(p_1 > p_2\).

"less"

H0: \(p_1 \ge p_2\) against H1: \(p_1 < p_2\).

Usage

test_difference(
  x1,
  n1,
  x2,
  n2,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  sensitivity = 1,
  specificity = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  icc = NULL,
  method = c("score", "wald")
)

Arguments

x1

Vector of whole-number counts of people who tested positive in group 1, one per site (a single number if group 1 is one site).

n1

Vector of whole-number totals tested in group 1, one per site (same length as x1).

x2

Vector of whole-number counts of people who tested positive in group 2, one per site (a single number if group 2 is one site).

n2

Vector of whole-number totals tested in group 2, one per site (same length as x2).

alternative

Direction of the test: "two.sided" (default), "greater" (group 1 higher) or "less" (group 1 lower).

sensitivity

Diagnostic sensitivity in (0, 1]; default 1. Assumed the same in both groups.

specificity

Diagnostic specificity in (0, 1]; default 1. Assumed the same in both groups. sensitivity + specificity must exceed 1.

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval on the difference, in (0, 1); default 0.95. The significance level of the test is 1 - conf_level.

icc

Optional. Intra-cluster correlation (ICC), in [0, 1]. If NULL (default), it is estimated separately for each group from its own sites. Otherwise give one number used for both groups, or two, c(group 1, group 2). A supplied value is also used for a group with only one site (see Details). Set to 0 for no clustering.

method

"score" (default): pooled z-test with the score interval. "wald": unpooled (Wald) z-test with the Wald interval. Each interval is its own test turned around, so the interval leaves out 0 exactly when reject is TRUE, whichever method is used.

Value

A list with:

difference

Estimated true difference, group 1 minus group 2: the measured difference divided by \(Se + Sp - 1\), between -1 and 1.

ci_lower, ci_upper

Confidence interval for the true difference; ci_upper is 1 for "greater" and ci_lower is -1 for "less".

p_value

p-value for the chosen alternative.

reject

TRUE if p_value is below 1 - conf_level.

prevalence1, prevalence2

Estimated true prevalence in each group (Rogan-Gladen corrected, between 0 and 1).

n_eff1, n_eff2

Effective sample size of each group, sum(n) / deff.

icc1, icc2

ICC used for each group: as supplied, or estimated from that group's data.

deff1, deff2

Design effect used for each group (1 with no clustering).

df

Degrees of freedom of the test (see Few sites); Inf when neither ICC is estimated.

Details

Design effect (returned as deff1 and deff2). For each group it is \(1 + (n_w - 1) ICC\), where \(n_w = \sum n^2 / \sum n\) is the mean number of people per site, weighted by site size. With icc supplied (for example from earlier surveys), that value is used. Supply icc for a group with one site only when the site stands for a wider population, such as a district; if the site itself is the population of interest, leave icc = NULL. With icc = NULL, the ICC of each group is estimated from its own data as in estimate_prevalence(); this needs at least two sites, and a group with one site gets a design effect of 1.

Few sites. An ICC estimated from \(k\) sites rests on only \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom, so the design effect is itself uncertain. When either group's ICC is estimated, the test statistic is compared with a t distribution in place of the normal, and the interval uses the matching t quantile. Its degrees of freedom (returned as df) combine the two groups by Satterthwaite's (1946) formula,

$$df = \frac{(v_1 + v_2)^2}{v_1^2 / df_1 + v_2^2 / df_2}, \qquad v_g = \hat{p}_g (1 - \hat{p}_g) / m_g$$

with \(df_g = k_g - 1\) for a group whose ICC is estimated, and a group whose ICC is supplied (or that has one site) left out of the denominator. With both ICCs supplied, df is Inf and the test is the normal one. In simulations with a true ICC of 0.1, 50 people per site and prevalences of 0.2 to 0.5, a 95 percent interval contained the true difference 96 to 97 percent of the time with 3 sites per group and 95 to 96 percent with 5. With 2 sites per group it is very wide (99 percent), an honest picture of how little 2 sites say.

Effective sample size. For group \(g\), \(m_g\) (returned as n_eff1 and n_eff2) is the number tested divided by the design effect.

Score test (method = "score"). With \(\hat{p}_g\) the measured prevalence in group \(g\),

$$z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} {\sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})\,(1/m_1 + 1/m_2)}}, \qquad \bar{p} = \frac{\hat{p}_1 m_1 + \hat{p}_2 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}.$$

With no clustering this is the same test as R's prop.test(correct = FALSE), and the one design_difference() sizes for.

Wald test (method = "wald"). The same, but with the standard error worked out from each group's own prevalence,

$$z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} {\sqrt{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)/m_1 + \hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)/m_2}}.$$

With small groups it can be too optimistic: with 20 people per group and true prevalences of 0.05 and 0.10, a 95 percent Wald interval contains the true difference only about 90 percent of the time (score 97). When each group's measured prevalence is 0 or 1 the standard error is 0.

For both, the one-sided p-values are the normal tail areas above and below \(z\) (t tail areas with df degrees of freedom when an ICC is estimated), and the two-sided p-value is twice the smaller of them.

Interval. The interval is the test turned around: it holds the differences \(\delta\) the test would not reject, so it leaves out 0 exactly when reject is TRUE. It matches alternative: two-sided for "two.sided", \([L, 1]\) for "greater" and \([-1, U]\) for "less".

For "score", the two prevalences are estimated again by maximum likelihood under the condition \(p_1 - p_2 = \delta\) (the closed form of Farrington and Manning, 1990), giving \(\tilde{p}_1, \tilde{p}_2\), and

$$z(\delta) = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 - \delta} {\sqrt{\tilde{p}_1(1-\tilde{p}_1)/m_1 + \tilde{p}_2(1-\tilde{p}_2)/m_2}}$$

is set equal to the z value for conf_level and solved for \(\delta\) (Mee, 1984). At \(\delta = 0\), \(\tilde{p}_1 = \tilde{p}_2 = \bar{p}\) and this is exactly the score test above. Miettinen and Nurminen (1985) multiply the variance by \((m_1 + m_2)/(m_1 + m_2 - 1)\); that factor is left out here so that the interval and the test always agree.

For "wald", the interval is \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \pm z \sqrt{\hat{p}_1(1 - \hat{p}_1)/m_1 + \hat{p}_2(1 - \hat{p}_2)/m_2}\).

The interval is built on the measured scale, then divided by \(Se + Sp - 1\) to give an interval for the true difference (the rest of the Rogan-Gladen correction cancels in a difference). Ends outside -1 to 1 are set to -1 or 1.

References

MMS-SD Study Design Workshop. https://mrc-ide.github.io/MMS-SD_workshop/

Fleiss, J. L., Levin, B. & Paik, M. C. (2003) Statistical Methods for Rates and Proportions, 3rd ed. Wiley. (Two-group z-test.)

Mee, R. W. (1984) Confidence bounds for the difference between two probabilities. Biometrics 40(4), 1175-1176.

Miettinen, O. & Nurminen, M. (1985) Comparative analysis of two rates. Statistics in Medicine 4(2), 213-226.

Farrington, C. P. & Manning, G. (1990) Test statistics and sample size formulae for comparative binomial trials with null hypothesis of non-zero risk difference or non-unity relative risk. Statistics in Medicine 9(12), 1447-1454. (Prevalences estimated under a given difference.)

Kish, L. (1965) Survey Sampling. Wiley. (Design effect.)

Satterthwaite, F. E. (1946) An approximate distribution of estimates of variance components. Biometrics Bulletin 2(6), 110-114. doi:10.2307/3002019

Rogan, W. J. & Gladen, B. (1978) Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology 107(1), 71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

Examples

# One count per group: 8 of 100 versus 20 of 120
test_difference(x1 = 8, n1 = 100, x2 = 20, n2 = 120)

#> [1] -0.08666667
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] -0.1746785
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.001913274
#>

#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $prevalence1
#> [1] 0.08
#> 
#> $prevalence2
#> [1] 0.1666667
#> 
#> $n_eff1
#> [1] 100
#> 
#> $n_eff2
#> [1] 120
#> 
#> $icc1
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $icc2
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff1
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $deff2
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] Inf
#> 

# Three sites per group, one-sided, imperfect diagnostic test. The sites
# differ, so the estimated design effects are above 1 (about 2.7 and 3.4)
# and p is 0.12; treating everyone as independent would give 0.007.
test_difference(
  x1 = c(1, 9, 3), n1 = c(50, 60, 40),
  x2 = c(4, 18, 9), n2 = c(55, 70, 45),
  alternative = "less",
  sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.97
)
